source: MITA 4.0 Maturity Model - PRA Pilot Update (April 2026)

level1.name: Initial
level1.description: SMA seeks to adopt enterprise-wide planning and architectural frameworks to improve program delivery. Current processes are unstructured, reactive, and inconsistent.

level2.name: Developing
level2.description: SMA complies with federal regulations and guidance and has begun adopting MES industry-recognized planning and architectural frameworks. Although basic processes and systems exist, they are not fully standardized or documented. The SMA collects and reports state-specific and MES metrics as well as performance data.

level3.name: Defined
level3.description: SMA complies with federal regulations and guidance and has fully implemented MES industry-recognized planning and architectural frameworks. Processes, systems, and strategies are standardized, well-documented, and aligned across the organization. The SMA actively monitors and analyzes state-specific and MES metrics as well as performance data for improvements.

level4.name: Managed
level4.description: SMA maintains compliance, follows industry-recognized planning and architectural frameworks, and monitors MES performance to meet goals. Processes are fully operational, consistent, and well executed. The SMA actively monitors and analyzes state-specific and MES metrics as well as performance data for improvements. The organization is a thought-leader in the MES ecosystem and actively collaborates and shares approaches with other SMAs.

level5.name: Optimized
level5.description: The SMA employs advanced, data-driven strategies to manage MES planning and architecture to align predictive decision-making with the SMA's long-term goals. Integrated processes, technologies, and data drive enterprise optimization. The SMA's institutionalized innovation supports adaptability, scalability, and continuous improvement. The organization is nationally recognized and actively collaborates and shares solutions with other SMAs.

notApplicable.name: Not Applicable
notApplicable.description: Not applicable was added by request of SMAs during listening sessions in late 2024. SMAs noted that some maturity criteria are inapplicable to their business operations or MES.

businessArchitecture.name: Business Architecture
businessArchitecture.description: The business processes performed to deliver the capability.

aspects.name: Business Process Performance
aspects.description: To what extent is the performance of business processes supporting this capability consistently measured, monitored, and managed using meaningful metrics?

level1.description: Business processes that support the capability are identified and defined, but performance expectations are implicit and not formally measured. Process outcomes vary and are not consistently reviewed.
questions: To what extent is the performance of business processes supporting this capability consistently measured, monitored, and managed using meaningful metrics?
evidence: Capability View: Capability mapped to supporting processes.
Process View: High‑level process definitions or catalog.
Artifacts: Process lists, capability maps, informal process descriptions.

level2.description: Business processes are documented in Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs), including steps and accountable roles. Performance expectations are understood informally but are not yet measured or tracked.
questions: To what extent is the performance of business processes supporting this capability consistently measured, monitored, and managed using meaningful metrics?
evidence: Process View: SOPs and Business Process Model with activities and role assignments.
Organization View: Role definitions linked to process steps.
Artifacts: Approved SOPs, role descriptions, training materials.

level3.description: Business processes are standardized and executed consistently across the organization. All staff follow the same documented process steps, and processes are centrally accessible through a Business Process Catalog.
questions: To what extent is the performance of business processes supporting this capability consistently measured, monitored, and managed using meaningful metrics?
evidence: Artifacts: Approved SOPs, role matrix, training materials.
Process View: Standardized BPMN or workflow models.

level4.description: Business processes have defined performance metrics (e.g., timeliness, quality, efficiency) that are regularly tracked, monitored, and reported. Process performance insights are used to identify bottlenecks and manage outcomes. Select steps may be automated to improve performance predictability.
questions: To what extent is the performance of business processes supporting this capability consistently measured, monitored, and managed using meaningful metrics?
evidence: Process View: End‑to‑end process models with KPIs.
Outcomes Based Planning Tool: Performance measures tied to outcomes.
Artifacts: KPI dashboards, performance reports, automation logs, leadership reviews.

level5.description: Business process performance is continuously assessed and optimized using metrics, trends, and feedback. Data‑driven insights are used to proactively improve effectiveness, efficiency, and capability outcomes through refinement, automation, and innovation.
questions: To what extent is the performance of business processes supporting this capability consistently measured, monitored, and managed using meaningful metrics?
evidence: Capability View: Performance trends tied to capability health.
Process View: Continuous improvement models and backlogs.
Artifacts: Process improvement roadmaps, trend analyses, root cause analyses, optimization initiatives, Improvement Plans,

aspects.name: Business Process Documentation
aspects.description: To what extent are the business processes that support this capability identified, documented using defined standards, centrally managed, and regularly maintained?

level1.description: Business processes that support the capability are partially or inconsistently identified. Process documentation is incomplete, informal, or outdated, and business process models are not fully developed or consistently used to guide execution.
questions: To what extent are the business processes that support this capability identified, documented using defined standards, centrally managed, and regularly maintained?
evidence: Partial lists of processes supporting the capability
Draft or outdated BPMs with gaps
Reliance on institutional  knowledge to understand processes

level2.description: All business processes supporting the capability are fully identified and documented. Business Process Models are developed for each process and are available for staff reference, but modeling quality and consistency may vary.
questions: To what extent are the business processes that support this capability identified, documented using defined standards, centrally managed, and regularly maintained?
evidence: Complete inventory of processes mapped to the capability. Process Catalog
BPMs available for all supporting processes
Process documentation used for onboarding or training

level3.description: Business processes supporting the capability are formally defined and documented using a common modeling standard (e.g., BPMN 2.0 or organization‑defined conventions), ensuring clarity, consistency, and adherence to industry best practices.
questions: To what extent are the business processes that support this capability identified, documented using defined standards, centrally managed, and regularly maintained?
evidence: BPMs compliant with BPMN 2.0 or internal standards
Periodic BPM quality or compliance assessments

level4.description: Business process documentation is managed in a standardized modeling tool that supports version control, change history, and traceability. Process models are maintained in an enterprise business process catalog with defined relationships to capabilities and metrics.
questions: To what extent are the business processes that support this capability identified, documented using defined standards, centrally managed, and regularly maintained?
evidence: Version history and change logs for BPMs
Documented relationships between processes, capabilities, and KPIs

level5.description: Business process documentation is managed in a standardized modeling tool that supports version control, change history, and traceability. Process models are maintained in an enterprise business process catalog with defined relationships to capabilities and metrics.
questions: To what extent are the business processes that support this capability identified, documented using defined standards, centrally managed, and regularly maintained?
evidence: Evidence of updates driven by metrics or insights
Process improvement logs or change requests
Alignment of BPM updates with capability or strategy changes

aspects.name: Business Process Governance
aspects.description: Are there individuals assigned to process governance roles that actively participate in the governance of the business process used to support this capability?

level1.description: Process governance roles and responsibilities have not been established or assigned to individuals for the business processes that support the capability.
questions: Are there individuals assigned to process governance roles that actively participate in the governance of the business process used to support this capability?

level2.description: Process governance roles and responsibilities for the business processes supporting the capability have been identified and assigned to individuals (e.g., capability/business owner, process owner), and key process terms, definitions, and acronyms used to support the capability have been identified and documented.
questions: Are there individuals assigned to process governance roles that actively participate in the governance of the business process used to support this capability?
evidence: Process Model View with Roles identified

level3.description: The SMA monitors the assignment of process governance roles to ensure minimal vacancy, and the assigned individuals actively participate in governing the business processes, including decision‑making related to process changes, standards, and alignment to the capability.
questions: Are there individuals assigned to process governance roles that actively participate in the governance of the business process used to support this capability?

level4.description: Process governance role assignments, process definitions, and key terms are stored in a central enterprise repository (e.g., business architecture or process catalog) and are accessible to stakeholders to search, discover, and understand the processes governed by the SMA.
questions: Are there individuals assigned to process governance roles that actively participate in the governance of the business process used to support this capability?

level5.description: Business processes adhere to enterprise process governance outcomes, policies, standards, and methodologies and are regularly assessed to identify opportunities to improve process governance, effectiveness, and alignment with the supported capability.
questions: Are there individuals assigned to process governance roles that actively participate in the governance of the business process used to support this capability?
evidence: Process Governance Diagram, SOPs, Process Governance Policy

aspects.name: Business Process Automation
aspects.description: To what extent are business processes that support this capability deliberately designed, automated, governed, measured, and continuously improved?

level1.description: Business Process automation is minimal or nonexistent. Processes supporting the capability are largely manual, with heavy reliance on spreadsheets, email, and individual workarounds.
questions: To what extent are business processes that support this capability deliberately designed, automated, governed, measured, and continuously improved?
evidence: Capability View: Capability defined at a high level with no automation attributes.
Process View: Informal process descriptions or institutional knowledge; no BPMN models.
Organization View: Roles implicit or unclear; automation ownership not defined.
Artifacts: Emails, spreadsheets, unstructured notes indicating manual execution.

level2.description: Isolated or tactical automation exists for parts of the process, often using basic tools or scripts. Automation efforts are reactive and focused on local efficiency rather than end‑to‑end capability support. Limited standards, reuse, or governance are applied.
questions: To what extent are business processes that support this capability deliberately designed, automated, governed, measured, and continuously improved?
evidence: Capability View: Capability decomposition includes partial automation support notes.
Process View: Documented subprocesses with point automation identified.
Organization View: Local ownership for automation initiatives.
Artifacts: Tool‑specific workflows, scripts, or low‑code apps with limited documentation.

level3.description: Automation is formally designed and standardized for key processes supporting the capability. Common tools and platforms are adopted, processes are mapped prior to automation, and automation follows defined patterns. Documentation, roles, and controls are established.
questions: To what extent are business processes that support this capability deliberately designed, automated, governed, measured, and continuously improved?
evidence: Capability View: Automation explicitly mapped to capabilities and outcomes.
Process View: Standardized BPMN models showing automated vs. manual steps.
Organization View: Defined roles for automation design, support, and ownership.
Information View: Inputs/outputs and data dependencies documented.
Artifacts: Approved process models, automation design standards, solution architecture diagrams.

level4.description: Automation is centrally governed, measured, and integrated across the capability. End‑to‑end processes are automated where appropriate, with performance metrics, monitoring, exception handling, and lifecycle management in place. Automation reliably supports business outcomes.
questions: To what extent are business processes that support this capability deliberately designed, automated, governed, measured, and continuously improved?
evidence: Capability View: Capability heatmaps showing automation maturity and performance.
Process View: End‑to‑end automated process models with controls and metrics.
Organization View: Clear governance structures and RACI models.
Artifacts: KPI dashboards, governance charters, operational metrics, exception reports.

level5.description: Automation is continuously optimized and intelligent. Advanced technologies (e.g., RPA, orchestration, low‑code, AI/ML) are leveraged to improve speed, quality, and adaptability. Data‑driven insights and continuous feedback loops drive ongoing capability enhancement and innovation.
questions: To what extent are business processes that support this capability deliberately designed, automated, governed, measured, and continuously improved?
evidence: Capability View: Continuous optimization tied to strategic capability outcomes.
Process View: Adaptive and event‑driven process models.
Information View: Analytics and feedback loops driving improvements.
Artifacts: Process mining insights, improvement backlogs, automation ROI analyses, AI‑enabled decision models.

aspects.name: Business Process Reporting
aspects.description: Are the reports that are created to support this process documented and traceable to the specific data used to create each report?

level1.description: Reports and measures that are produced to support this process have not been identified and documented.
questions: Are the reports that are created to support this process documented and traceable to the specific data used to create each report?

level2.description: Reports and measures that are produced to support this process have been identified and documented.
questions: Are the reports that are created to support this process documented and traceable to the specific data used to create each report?

level3.description: Reports and measure standards have been established and implemented and are delivered to key stakeholders to support this process
questions: Are the reports that are created to support this process documented and traceable to the specific data used to create each report?

level4.description: Detailed measure specifications and report definitions have been documented and are tracked to the impacted information used to produce the measure and report in a central metadata repository.
questions: Are the reports that are created to support this process documented and traceable to the specific data used to create each report?

level5.description: Reports and measures that are used to support this process adhere to enterprise business intelligence processes, procedures, standards, metadata and technology and are regularly assessed to improve the quality of the reports and measures.
questions: Are the reports that are created to support this process documented and traceable to the specific data used to create each report?

enterpriseArchitecture.name: Enterprise Architecture

level3.description: The SMA has fully documented and defined the capability roles, supporting processes, technology and information. The capability complies with state and federal requirements and the conforms to MES industry - recognized architectural frameworks. The capability is standardized and aligned at the enterprise level.
questions: To what extent are business capabilities  defined, documented, governed, measured, and improved to support the enterprise?
evidence: Performance Metricss, MITA SS-A, Central EA repository

level4.description: The SMA manages the capability for performance and compliance. The SMA monitors the metrics and measures of the capability.

questions: To what extent are business capabilities  defined, documented, governed, measured, and improved to support the enterprise?

level2.description: SMA complies with federal guidance and has begun adopting MES-recognized EA frameworks. EA processes exist but are not standardized or fully documented.

level3.description: SMA has fully implemented MES-recognized EA frameworks. EA processes are standardized, documented, and aligned across business, information and technology.
questions: To what extent is enterprise architecture  integrated into MITA enterprise planning, governance,  and execution to guide and optimize business, information, and technology outcomes?

level4.description: SMA uses EA to monitor and manage MES performance. EA is integrated into strategic planning and execution. SMA collaborates with other SMAs to share EA practices.

level5.description: SMA uses advanced, data-driven EA strategies for proactive decision-making. EA drives enterprise optimization and continuous improvement. SMA is nationally recognized for EA leadership.
questions: To what extent is enterprise architecture  integrated into MITA enterprise planning, governance,  and execution to guide and optimize business, information, and technology outcomes?

aspects.name: Policy Management
aspects.description: To what extent are policies systematically integrated into enterprise architecture, capability planning, and governance processes to guide compliance, decision‑making, and execution within MITA?

level1.description: Policies relevant to business capabilities are informally identified or inconsistently documented. There is little to no mapping of policies to business processes or systems.
questions: To what extent are policies systematically integrated into enterprise architecture, capability planning, and governance processes to guide compliance, decision‑making, and execution within MITA?

level2.description: Some policies are documented and beginning to be mapped to business processes and systems. Compliance is mostly reactive, and regular reviews are not established.
questions: To what extent are policies systematically integrated into enterprise architecture, capability planning, and governance processes to guide compliance, decision‑making, and execution within MITA?

level3.description: All business policies relevant to the capability (e.g., "Pharmacy Management") are identified, documented, and mapped to business processes and supporting systems. Policies are harmonized with state and federal requirements, and their alignment is regularly reviewed to ensure compliance and support for enterprise objectives.
questions: To what extent are policies systematically integrated into enterprise architecture, capability planning, and governance processes to guide compliance, decision‑making, and execution within MITA?
evidence: Policy/Process/Technology Component Matrix, Policy and Strategy Catalogs

level4.description: Policy alignment is institutionalized and integrated into enterprise governance. Policies are systematically reviewed, updated, and optimized based on performance data, regulatory changes, and strategic objectives.
questions: To what extent are policies systematically integrated into enterprise architecture, capability planning, and governance processes to guide compliance, decision‑making, and execution within MITA?
evidence: Performance Metricss, MITA SS-A, Central policy repository

level5.description: Policy alignment is a proactive, continuous process that drives organizational agility, compliance, and innovation. The organization demonstrates thought leadership and collaborates externally to share best practices.
questions: To what extent are policies systematically integrated into enterprise architecture, capability planning, and governance processes to guide compliance, decision‑making, and execution within MITA?
evidence: Outcomes based Planning Tool, Goal, Driver, Objective Catalog

aspects.name: Strategic Planning
aspects.description: To what extent is the SMA’s strategic planning formally integrated into enterprise architecture, capability planning, and governance processes to guide the execution  of MITA?

level1.description: The SMA’s strategic plan is informally considered during architecture and capability planning efforts. Alignment between strategy and capabilities occurs opportunistically and is largely dependent on individual initiative rather than a defined planning approach.
questions: To what extent is the SMA’s strategic planning formally integrated into enterprise architecture, capability planning, and governance processes to guide the execution  of MITA?

level2.description: The SMA’s strategic plan and capability planning are intentionally aligned through defined outcomes. Strategic objectives inform capability discussions, but dependencies between strategy, capabilities, and processes are not yet consistently analyzed or governed.
questions: To what extent is the SMA’s strategic planning formally integrated into enterprise architecture, capability planning, and governance processes to guide the execution  of MITA?
evidence: Outcomes Catalog, Outcomes Based Planning Tool

level3.description: The SMA’s strategic plan explicitly identifies capabilities as required dependencies to achieve strategic outcomes. Capabilities and supporting processes are identified and analyzed as part of Enterprise Portfolio and Project Management to inform prioritization and planning decisions.
questions: To what extent is the SMA’s strategic planning formally integrated into enterprise architecture, capability planning, and governance processes to guide the execution  of MITA?
evidence: Process Catalog, Capability Catalog, Enterprise Portfolio, Metrics Catalog

level4.description: The SMAs Enterprise Roadmap(Projects/Initiatives) have capabilities and processes identified that support the roadmap items. Capabilities and Process are identified and analyzed for intake of new business to support funding requests for an APD, or state funding for project approval
questions: To what extent is the SMA’s strategic planning formally integrated into enterprise architecture, capability planning, and governance processes to guide the execution  of MITA?

level5.description: Capabilities and processes are core inputs to enterprise governance and decision‑making. Strategic planning, investment decisions, and roadmap prioritization are consistently driven by capability and process analysis to ensure alignment, maximize value, and support execution of SMA strategic objectives.
questions: To what extent is the SMA’s strategic planning formally integrated into enterprise architecture, capability planning, and governance processes to guide the execution  of MITA?

technology.name: Technology
technology.description: The technology infrastructure and application architecture supporting the capability.

subDimensions.name: Technology Infrastructure Management
subDimensions.description: Assess the Technical Architecture maturity of the Medicaid Enterprise System (MES).

aspects.name: Compute and Storage
aspects.description: Does the MES have servers on premise, hybrid, or cloud with routine, scheduled backup?

level1.description: The MES uses physical servers, with little or no virtualization, with backup and storage is addressed ad-hoc.
questions: Are most MES servers physical?
Are backups performed manually?
evidence: Infrastructure diagrams, server inventory, operations documentation

level2.description: Some virtualization is used for the MES, with servers provisioned manually and storage and backups scheduled.
questions: Is the MES using virtualization?
Are backups scheduled and monitored?
evidence: Infrastructure diagrams, server inventory, operations documentation

level3.description: The MES is on premise and cloud environment, with resources provisioned through standard configurations and scripting, and automated backups of business-critical data.
questions: Does the MES use cloud hosting for some services?
Do backups adhere to a retention schedule?

level4.description: The MES uses cloud-based environments that are governed through standardized templates, and automation is used to manage storage and backups for growth, volume, and retention.
questions: Does the MES provision servers and storage through automation?
Are MES server and storage costs reviewed?
evidence: Cost / Utilization metrics, documentation of reviews and decisions made

level5.description: The MES has cloud compute and hosting infrastructure across environments, immutable backups are retained based on retention schedule, compute / storage usage and cost thresholds defined and regularly reviewed.
questions: Is the MES cloud native?
Are storage and backups immutable and retention automated?
evidence: Storage and backup documentation and automation processes

aspects.name: Networking and Technical Recovery
aspects.description: Does the MES have network segmentation that is regularly tested for outages and recovery?

level1.description: The MES is a flat network, with limited monitoring for network traffic, and unplanned outages that are manually resolved.
questions: Does the MES have network segmentation?
Is there a documented technical recovery approach?

level2.description: The MES has some segmentation and network traffic logs are reviewed, manual testing of failovers and restorations occurs.
questions: Are resources in place to manage network traffic securely?
Are technical recovery plans annually tested?
evidence: Network architecture diagram, network access documentation
Technical Recovery Testing Schedule and results

level3.description: The MES has network segmentation, with defined networking patterns, and Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO) defined in Service Level Agreements (SLAs).
questions: Does the MES network have standardization across environments?
Does the technical recovery approach have metrics defined?

level4.description: The MES monitors network traffic and has adopted standard patterns, and scheduled testing of failover and restoration of services regularly occurs, with SLAs monitored and reported.
questions: Is network performance and alerting available and implemented?
Are technical recovery plans regularly tested and recovery measured against metrics?
evidence: Technical Recovery Testing Schedule and results

level5.description: The MES network is proactively reviewed, and network performance is continuously optimized during peak usage, and the MES has automated failover and restoration ability, with redundancy of environments and limited or no user impact.
questions: Is automation and advanced networking in place?
Are system outages proactively mitigated?

aspects.name: Identity, Access, and Consent
aspects.description: Does the MES have identity, access, and consent services for internal and external users?

level1.description: The MES has limited ability to manage user identity and access, and consent is captured manually for Medicaid applicants and members.
questions: Are accounts and access manually provisioned?
Is consent captured manually?

level2.description: The MES has user identity and access standardized for new systems and some systems capture consent for Medicaid applicants and members, and consent revocation is manual.
questions: Are account management processes defined?
Is consent revocation captured manually?
evidence: Identity management, verification, and access request process documentation

level3.description: The MES uses centralized identity and access management for most applications with Roles Based Access Control (RBAC), and Medicaid applicant and member consent, preferences, and revocation is collected and auditable within most Medicaid applications in the MES.
questions: Is Roles Based Access Control in place for the MES and managed centrally?
Is consent and revocation electronically captured?
evidence: RBAC documentation, identity management architecture diagram

level4.description: The MES uses centralized identity and access management, RBAC, and activities are logged, auditable,  with Medicaid applicant and member consent, preferences, and revocation centrally managed.
questions: Are user identity and access automated and audited?
Is Consent centrally managed?

level5.description: The MES integrates entify and access management across internal and external systems and organizations, with continuous improvement and automation, and Medicaid applicant and member consent, preferences, and revocation are user managed, and shared across internal and external MES systems and Medicaid organizations.
questions: Is identity and access management integrated across internal and external systems and organizations?
Is member consent and revocation of member or applicant defined and shared across systems?

aspects.name: Security Protection and Monitoring
aspects.description: Does the MES have security controls, with incident logging and monitoring?

level1.description: The MES has security controls inconsistently applied, and security monitoring is inconsistent with limited visibility and alerting.
questions: Are security controls drafted?
Is monitoring siloed or inconsistent?

level2.description: The MES has security controls defined and partially implemented, monitoring and alerts are manually reviewed.
questions: Are security processes defined?
Are security monitoring guidelines defined?

level3.description: The MES has security controls that are implemented across Medicaid applications, with data encrypted, and monitoring and logs are reviewed.
questions: Are security controls implemented across the MES?
Are internal security audits conducted?
Are alerts and logs collected?
evidence: Security diagrams and security control inventory

level4.description: The MES has consistently implemented security controls, regular auditing, and automated checks and security events or incidents alerting.
questions: Are security controls monitored and updated for the MES?
Are security event or incident plans tested?
evidence: Security Diagrams, security control monitoring logs

level5.description: The MES has security controls that are continuously optimized, audited, and validated, and monitoring supports compliance and audit readiness, exceeding federal and state regulatory expectations.
questions: Do security controls meet or exceed state and federal regulatory expectations?
Are threat analytics reviewed proactively?
evidence: Security control inventory and monitoring logs

aspects.name: System Operations and Monitoring
aspects.description: Does the MES have standard operating practices and monitoring of performance?

level1.description: The MES has manual operations with limited documentation with system logs reviewed for performance.
questions: Are system operations documented?
Is monitoring limited to specific applications or environments?

level2.description: The MES has manual operations with partial process and procedure documentation and guidelines for monitoring performance.
questions: Are system operation processes documented?
Are monitoring and alerting standards defined?

level3.description: The MES has operations that follow internal procedures with service level agreements, and alerts and monitoring of MES application performance and health.
questions: Is the quality of system operations defined and measured?
Is monitoring and alerting implemented?
evidence: System operations documentation, SLAs with metrics
Monitoring and alerting rules, documentation, and diagrams

level4.description: The MES has operations that follow industry standard processes, are automated where feasible, with monitoring and alerting integrated with systems operations.
questions: Are system operation processes automated where feasible?
Is monitoring and alerting automated for critical applications?
evidence: System operations documentation, with SLA and metrics
Monitoring and alerting rules, documentation, and diagrams

level5.description: The MES has operations that are benchmarked and continuously improved and aligned with industry standard processes, monitoring and alerting analytics are centralized for MES application performance and health
questions: Are system operations fully automated, aligned with SLAs, and continually improved?
Is monitoring and alerting automated and centralized?
evidence: System operations documentation with SLA and metrics
Monitoring and alerting rules, documentation, and diagrams

aspects.name: Development, Testing, Release, and Security Compliance
aspects.description: Does the MES have centralized source and script management with testing and security reviews?

level1.description: The MES has no version control of source code or scripts, manual testing, and limited security compliance checks.

Is testing manual?
Are security reviews inconsistent?
evidence: Security review checklist, development documentation including secure coding standards

level2.description: The MES has basic version control of source code or scripts, releases and testing follow checklists, and manual security compliance reviews occur.
questions: Is version control of source code and scripts used for some systems?
Are testing activities repeatable across teams?
Is security review included in testing?
evidence: Testing process documentation, testing checklists, records from prior application security testing

level3.description: The MES has standardized version control of source code and scripts, pre-production environments are defined, release and testing procedures are defined, and security reviews are standardized.
questions: Is version control of source code and scripts standardized across all teams?
Are release procedures used?
Are secure coding standards implemented?
evidence: Development and configuration procedures, environment architecture
Development documentation including secure coding standards

level4.description: The MES has centralized version control of source code and scripts, release and testing are automated across pre-production environments, testing metrics are reviewed, and security reviews occur with release planning.
questions: Is version control of source code and scripts centralized?
Are pre-production environments in place with release automation?
Are security reviews part of release planning?
evidence: Environment diagrams and release workflow documentation

level5.description: The MES has automated source code and script management, releases are continuous across pre-production and production environments, releases are monitored, and continuous security reviews and compliance are performed.
questions: Is source code and script version control automated?
Are releases continuously deployed across pre-production and production environments as applicable?
Are continuous security and compliance reviews automated during development? and compliance in place?
evidence: Development, configuration, and release process documentation

outcomes.name: Organizational Outcomes
outcomes.description: The definition of the desired outcomes that require the capability to be achieved.

aspects.name: Culture & Mindset
aspects.description: Organizational norms, expectations, and behaviors related to outcome development.

level1.description: No culture or expectation of outcomes for projects (at any phase of the project).

level2.description: Recognition begins to take hold of the importance of outcomes during planning.

level3.description: Leadership sets expectations; outcome development during planning becomes a norm.

level4.description: Outcome development is formalized and institutionally expected.

level5.description: Outcome thinking is fully embedded at all levels of organization—without direction by or requirement from leadership.

aspects.name: Capability
aspects.description: The internal capacity to develop, oversee, and apply outcomes without reliance on vendors.

level1.description: No internal capabilities to identify or draft outcomes.

level2.description: Organization understands at a high-level what elements are needed to identify and draft outcomes, but vendor leads development of outcomes.

level3.description: Sufficient experience in identifying and drafting outcomes internally; organization may lead or closely oversee vendors to draft outcomes.

level4.description: Full in-house capability to independently produce outcomes.

level5.description: Deep in-house expertise with fully self-sufficient teams across the organization. Organization may also support sister organizations and agencies in developing outcomes.

aspects.name: Quality & Consistency
aspects.description: The clarity, structure, and strategic alignment of outcome statements.

level1.description: Outcomes are ambiguous, inconsistent, and disconnected from goals. No consistent approach or methodology to developing outcomes.

level2.description: Outcomes may be aligned with priorities but are not 'smart' or actionable. Defined approach or methodology to developing outcomes.

level3.description: Outcomes capture the capability sought and benefit derived from a given project, but the quality of the outcome statements vary. Well-established and consistently applied approach to developing outcomes.

level4.description: Outcomes are clear, actionable, reusable, and strategically aligned. Well-established and consistently applied approach to developing outcomes.

level5.description: Outcome statements are of consistently high quality, recognizable, and standardized.

aspects.name: Alignment to Goals & Priorities
aspects.description: The extent to which outcomes are traceable to broader goals, priorities, and mission.

level1.description: Outcomes are not aligned to goals or priorities.

level2.description: Emerging awareness of need to align outcomes with goals and priorities but gaps remain.

level3.description: Outcomes are intentionally aligned to strategic goals and priorities.

level4.description: Systematic alignment of outcomes to goals and priorities. Outcomes inform broader strategies.

level5.description: Outcomes reflect and reinforce strategic direction seamlessly.

aspects.name: Use of Metrics
aspects.description: How outcomes are tracked, and metrics are used to measure progress and guide improvement.

level1.description: No recognition of the need to measure progress toward achieving outcomes or commitment to continuous improvement.

level2.description: Interest in measuring progress toward achieving outcomes. Metrics are not well-aligned with outcomes.

level3.description: Metrics are generally appropriate and regularly referenced to determine progress in achieving outcomes. Some engagement in continuous improvement cycles.

level4.description: Metrics are well-developed. Staff regularly use metrics to evaluate performance and engage in well-established continuous improvement cycles.

level5.description: Performance monitoring is deeply embedded in organization's culture. Metrics and outcomes support continuous improvement, learning, and decision-making.

aspects.name: Reusability & Integration
aspects.description: Whether outcomes are reused across project documents, Advance Planning Documents (APD), systems, and reporting.

level1.description: No reuse. Outcomes are informal or nonexistent.

level2.description: Reuse is isolated to APDs; no reuse across other project, planning, or leadership documents.

level3.description: Reuse is focused on APDs and some project-related documents. Inconsistent reuse across leadership documents, and external communications.

level4.description: Reuse is consistent and intentional across APDs, project documents, and leadership and external communications.

level5.description: Seamless reuse across systems and communications, which improves coherence and efficiency.

roles.name: Organizational Roles
roles.description: The individual roles responsible for providing the capability.

aspects.name: Technology Resources
aspects.description: Management and understanding of technical resources across the SMA.

level1.description: Partial list of technical resources exists; capabilities are not fully understood across the SMA.

level2.description: SMA maintains a comprehensive list of all technical resources and their capabilities.

level3.description: SMA maps technical resources directly to business processes.

level4.description: Technical resources are actively shared and optimized across business units for seamless execution.

level5.description: Technical resources are accessible to agencies, states, and federal partners and support continuous improvement through data-driven insights and collaborative efforts; drives technical reforms across the broader health and human services network.

aspects.name: Organizational Goals Alignment
aspects.description: Alignment of business units with enterprise-wide Medicaid goals.

level1.description: Business units operate in silos without clear understanding of enterprise-wide Medicaid goals.

level2.description: Organizational goals are defined but not fully communicated across all levels.

level3.description: Business units align their roles and processes to support broader Medicaid goals.

level4.description: All roles (internal and external) collaborate to drive enterprise-wide Medicaid program goals, with regular reassessments for alignment.

level5.description: SMA leadership collaborates at the national level to set adaptable, data-driven goals and performance outcomes for the Medicaid program; focus is on improving healthcare and social services delivery and beneficiary well-being nationwide.

aspects.name: Governance & Standardization
aspects.description: Formal governance structures and process standardization.

level1.description: Limited or no formal governance to guide roles or standardize processes.

level2.description: Some governance exists, but role clarity and process standardization are inconsistent.

level3.description: Formal governance structures support role clarity, with standard operating procedures (SOP).

level4.description: Enterprise governance bodies actively coordinate roles, processes, and data for continuous improvement and standardization.

level5.description: SMA leads data-driven solutions at a national level and collaborates with other SMAs to develop shared business and technical standards that are disseminated nationally to strengthen overall Medicaid service delivery.

aspects.name: Communication (Internal / External)
aspects.description: Communication channels between leadership, business, and technical units.

level1.description: Minimal communication between leadership, business, and technical units.

level2.description: Defined communication channels exist but are not used consistently.

level3.description: Regular cross-unit communication occurs, including with external partners like Managed Care Organizations (MCO) and vendors.

level4.description: Transparent, enterprise-wide communication ensures all roles understand priorities, responsibilities, and impacts.

level5.description: Integrates communication across all business areas to align long-term Medicaid goals and performance outcomes. Fosters cooperation with other SMAs, CMS, and external partners nationally. The Agency is recognized for its leadership in sharing solutions, provider enrollment process needs, and best practices.

aspects.name: Culture & Leadership
aspects.description: Leadership visibility into workloads and resource capacity.

level1.description: Leadership lacks visibility into workloads and resource capacity; roles are reactive.

level2.description: Leadership begins assessing role capacity but lacks full enterprise insight.

level3.description: Leadership proactively manages workloads and roles based on enterprise needs and priorities.

level4.description: Leadership fosters a culture of collaboration and continuous learning across internal and external roles.

level5.description: Leadership supports internal change agents to align culture, strategy, and resources with long-term Medicaid goals.

aspects.name: Resourcing Capacity (Staffing, Training, Recruitment)
aspects.description: Capacity management for staffing, training, and recruitment.

level1.description: SMA struggles to identify gaps in role capacity; staffing is reactive.

level2.description: Some processes exist for role capacity management (staffing, training, recruitment).

level3.description: SMA systematically identifies, recruits, and trains staff.

level4.description: SMA maintains a dynamic capacity model to forecast and meet enterprise role needs, including succession planning and continuous role development.

level5.description: SMA uses comprehensive planning and advanced analytics to align roles and skills with program objectives, enabling rapid response to required changes while maintaining high service delivery standards.
